own_scenes.desc: Europa mantenía una relación a distancia con el concepto de Detroit codificado en los vinilos, y en 313, la lista de correo del techno de Detroit, fans de decenas de países aprendían y se obsesionaban con la ciudad. En diciembre de 1999 sus miembros hicieron una fiesta en Redford, a la que viajaron músicos holandeses como Hans Veneman, Otto Koppius, Wibo Lammerts y Klaas-Jan Jongsma; volvieron en 2000 para el festival y alguien los bautizó «techno tourists» (technotourist.org), que recopilaba todas las fiestas posteriores. Un modelo para la siguiente generación de fans, que coleccionan y comparten experiencias en lugar de vagar como tribus ravers.

refs.q: Yes, the capital of the post-industrial Midwest was becoming a vacation destination—for young people.
refs.para: Like all long-distance love affairs, there has to be a moment where the need for intimacy overwhelms. For Detroit, this meant that the techno “massive,” as it were, began to visit. Yes, the capital of the post-industrial Midwest was becoming a vacation destination—for young people. 313 was an early facilitator, as many music mailing lists with similar early 1990s histories were functional extensions of the rave community. Whereas most are very local in scope, such as sf-raves, mw-raves, and ne-raves (San Francisco, Midwest, and Northeast respectively), 313’s reach is global. Bits finally gave way to atoms in December 1999, where a party by and for 313 list members was held in the Detroit suburb of Redford. In attendance were several international visitors, including Otto Koppius, Hans Veneman, Wibo Lammerts, and Klaas-Jan Jongsma—all musicians and DJs who made the trek from the Netherlands.
